title: Sujebi
subtitle: Hand-torn flour dough soup with vegetables
excerpt: A simple dough is rested, then torn into thin, irregular pieces directly into a simmering anchovy stock loaded with potato, courgette and carrot. The torn dough pieces cook into chewy, soft dumplings that absorb the flavour of the broth. This recipe serves 4 and takes around 40 minutes. It is a beloved Korean comfort food with no specialist equipment required.
sourceNotes: Sujebi has been made in Korean households for centuries as an economical and filling meal when rice was scarce. The hand-torn technique is entirely intentional: the irregular, rough edges of the torn dough create more surface area to absorb the broth and give the pieces their characteristic chewy texture. It was historically a food of the countryside and lean times, now widely loved across Korea.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be made up to an hour ahead and kept covered at room temperature. Do not refrigerate or it becomes too stiff to tear thinly.

glossaryTerms.definition: Sujebi is a Korean hand-torn dough soup, sometimes described as a Korean version of pasta e fagioli or a dumpling soup. The name comes from the method rather than the ingredients: 'su' relates to hands and 'jebi' to the act of tearing. The dough is made simply from flour and water, rested briefly, then torn into thin, roughly shaped pieces directly into simmering broth. The irregular edges are part of what makes the texture distinctive.

In sujebi, the dough is torn rather than cut. Take a small piece of dough, flatten it between your fingers until it is roughly 2mm thick and irregularly shaped, then drop it directly into the boiling broth. The thinness is more important than the shape. Thinner pieces cook quickly and remain soft rather than doughy in the centre. Work in batches so the broth stays at a simmer.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 40 minutes in total including the dough resting time.
is one of the few Korean recipes that asks you to make fresh dough, but the dough is as simple as it gets: just flour and water. The skill lies entirely in the
, which takes one or two attempts to get right.

Rest the dough for at least 15 minutes after mixing. A rested dough is far more pliable and easier to stretch thin between your fingers. If the dough springs back immediately when you try to flatten it, it needs more resting time. Tear small portions at a time and keep the rest covered with cling film so it does not dry out.

Make the dough. Place the flour in a bowl and add the warm water a little at a time, mixing with a fork or your hands until a rough dough comes together. Knead briefly until smooth, then wrap in cling film and rest at room temperature for 15 to 20 minutes.
Make the anchovy stock. Place the dried anchovies in a large saucepan with the 1.5 litres of water. Bring to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes. Remove and discard the anchovies.
Add the potato, garlic and soy sauce to the anchovy stock. Bring back to the boil and simmer for 5 minutes.

Add the courgette and carrot. Keep the soup at a steady simmer. Now begin tearing the dough. Take a walnut-sized piece, flatten it between your thumbs and fingers until it is thin and roughly 4 to 5cm across, then drop it directly into the simmering broth. Repeat until all the dough is used.
Cook for 5 to 7 minutes after the last piece of dough has gone in, until the dough pieces are cooked through and no longer floury in the centre. They will float to the surface when done.
Add the spring onions in the final minute. Season with salt to taste. Drizzle with sesame oil and serve immediately in deep bowls.

items.symptom: Dough pieces are thick and doughy in the centre
items.cause: The pieces were not torn thin enough before dropping into the soup
items.fix: Each piece should be stretched to roughly 2mm thick before going into the broth. Hold it up to the light and it should be thin enough to see your fingers through. Thicker pieces need more cooking time.

items.symptom: Dough pieces stick together in a mass in the pot
items.cause: Too many pieces were added at once or the broth was not simmering vigorously enough
items.fix: Tear and add the pieces one or two at a time, giving each one a moment before adding the next. Keep the broth at a steady simmer so the pieces move around freely.

items.symptom: Soup tastes flat despite the anchovy stock
items.cause: The anchovies were not simmered for long enough to release their flavour
items.fix: Simmer the anchovies for a full 10 minutes and taste the stock before adding vegetables. If it still tastes weak, add an extra tablespoon of soy sauce or a pinch more salt.

content.text: Sujebi is a rainy-day dish in Korea. It is the thing people make when they are at home, it is cold outside, and they want something filling and warm that does not require a trip to the shops for specialist ingredients. It has the status of simple, nourishing home cooking rather than a restaurant dish. Children grow up eating it and continue making it as adults for the same reason their parents did.
